messages.text: Look, I've had the property appraised and the new market rate for this unit is 2400 a month. That's what I'm going to need going forward when your lease comes up for renewal.
That's a pretty steep jump from what I'm paying now. What am I at currently, like $1800? That's a 33% increase — I need to understand what's driving that.

Property taxes went up, insurance premiums jumped, and frankly the market has moved significantly in this area. I'm not the one setting these prices — the market is, and 2400 is what comparable units are going for right now.

I get that costs go up, but I've been a reliable tenant here for years — no late payments, no complaints. When I look at what's actually available in the building and the neighborhood, I'm seeing units more in the 2000 to 2100 range. That's still a solid increase from what I'm paying, but it's more in line with reality than 2400.

I appreciate you being a good tenant, I really do, but reliable tenants are a dime a dozen when the market's hot like this. Those comps you're looking at might be older listings or smaller units. I need 2400 to make the numbers work on this property.

Look, I've done my homework on those comps — they're current and they're similar units. I understand you need to make money, but I'm not going to pay 33% more just because the market shifted. I can do 2150, maybe 2175 if you want to sweeten it a bit, but 2400 is just too much for me to absorb.

I hear you, but 2150 is below what I need to cover my costs on this place. I can come down to 2200 and that's really as low as I can go — that still gives you some relief from the 2400 ask, and it keeps you in the unit.

2200 is still a pretty big jump for me — that's a 22% increase. Look, I want to stay here, but I also need this to be sustainable on my end. Can you walk me through what those actual costs are? Because if I can see the numbers, maybe we can find some middle ground around 2075, 2100.

I'm not going to break down my operating costs line by line — that's not how this works. You either want to stay here at 2200 or you don't, but I'm not negotiating on my financials. What I will tell you is that 2200 is my final number.

I appreciate you laying it out, but that doesn't really help me here. Look, I can probably stretch to 2125 — that's a meaningful concession on my part and it shows good faith. But 2200 is genuinely tough for me to make work month to month.
Look, I get that it's tight for you, but 2200 is where I need to be. I've already moved from my asking price, and I can't go any lower than that without losing money on this unit every month.

I hear you, and I know you've moved from 2400. But asking me to absorb a 22% increase is a lot. If 2200 is truly your floor, then I need to think about whether I can actually make that work long-term, or if I need to start looking at other options. Can you give me a few days to figure out my budget?

Sure, take a few days if you need to, but understand that if you walk, I'll re-list this unit at 2400 and it'll rent in a week. The market's moving fast right now. Let me know by Friday what you want to do.

Yeah, I understand — the market's hot. Look, I'll crunch the numbers and get back to you by Friday. But just so we're clear, if I'm staying, I need something closer to 2150. If you won't budge below 2200, then we might not have a deal, and we'll both move on.
That's fair — you do what you need to do. But I'm telling you straight, 2200 is as low as I go. Call me Friday and we'll see where we're at.
